problems.description: Measured convention score is 0.70 (16 violations), but nearly all listed violations reference files outside this commit (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, conftest.py) — pre-existing baseline debt, not introduced here; only 'app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' touches this diff and is itself dubious since app.py adds no classes.

tests/test_app.py uses a sys.path.insert(0, ...) hack and mutates the module-level DATABASE global in the fixture rather than relying on a package/conftest setup; works but is a testing anti-pattern that couples tests to module layout.

The 422/404 JSON error responses are now implemented twice — via errorhandlers for Flask-generated errors and inline jsonify(error) returns in route bodies — risking drift if the response shape changes.

strengths: Centralizes status validation in a single VALID_STATUSES constant instead of inlining magic strings
Adds consistent JSON 404/405 error handlers, keeping the API's response shape uniform
Comprehensive test suite (13 tests) covering create/list/get/update, empty/missing titles, invalid status (with unchanged-state assertion), and not-found cases
Change is minimal and surgical (+149/-1 lines), staying inside the existing Flask/jsonify idiom
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested greenfield session that adds input validation and uniform error handling to a Flask API; the measured 0.70 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touches.

problems.description: app.py:31 silently falls back to a hardcoded SECRET_KEY when the env var is unset, so any deployment missing it signs forgeable JWT tokens; acceptable as a loud dev default but should be required (assert/error) in production.

Ownership enforcement lives only at the route layer (app.py owner_id checks in show_task/edit_task); the model helper update_task() does not scope by owner, so a future non-route caller could mutate another user's task.

Auth, migration, and task logic all remain in the single app.py file; consistent with the baseline's single-file design, but the surface area is growing and may warrant extracting models/routes as the story progresses.

Pre-auth tasks keep owner_id = NULL (documented in _migrate_add_owner_id), making existing rows invisible to all users; acceptable and intentional, but it is a silent data-visibility change for anyone relying on the old all-tasks view.

The 0.70 repo convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit did not touch (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, conftest.py); the diff's own code follows snake_case, section-banner, type-hint, and with get_db() conventions.

strengths: Clean backward-compatible migration (_migrate_add_owner_id) that adds owner_id via PRAGMA introspection and preserves existing rows instead of rebuilding the table.
Foreign-task access returns 404 rather than 403, avoiding resource-existence leaks.
Consistent with existing patterns: with get_db() context, section banners, get_json(silent=True), jsonify error shape, snake_case, and type hints on public helpers.
Proper auth hygiene: werkzeug password hashing (no plaintext), JWT exp claim with 24h TTL, and explicit expired/invalid-token error handling.
Substantial test growth (+358 lines, 32 new functions per AST diff) covering the new auth and ownership behavior.
commit_reviews.summary: Adds clean JWT auth with owner-scoped task isolation and strong test coverage while faithfully following the baseline's single-file patterns, incurring only minor debt from a dev-default secret key and route-layer-only ownership enforcement.

problems.description: A full Celery + Redis broker/result-backend stack is introduced solely to dispatch a notification email that is mocked (prints to stdout). This adds a persistent process (worker) and an external Redis dependency to a simple synchronous Flask+SQLite API, for functionality with no real delivery path — severe over-engineering for the stated requirement.

The 'completed' alias status creates two distinct statuses ('done'/'completed') encoding the same domain state. The explicit comment confirms this exists only to trigger the notification, which means the domain model now carries redundancy that can drift in future queries/reports instead of triggering on the pre-existing 'done' transition.

app.py imports celery_app at module import time, so the Flask app becomes import-dependent on Celery/Redis packages; broker defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0, and the app will fail to start or import if the broker is unreachable, with no lazy import or fallback.

Convention score 0.70 with 16 violations, concentrated in the two new modules: module-level constants (broker_url, result_backend, celery_app instance config) should be UPPER_CASE per the codebase style.

Duplications +7.0%: the new test module repeats register/login/auth_header helper blocks and fixture boilerplate verbatim rather than reusing conftest.py fixtures, and resorts to a sys.path.insert hack for imports.

Cognitive complexity +5: the inline notification branch inside edit_task couples persistence logic with side-effecting dispatch; a small helper (e.g. notify_on_completion) would keep the endpoint single-purpose.
The 'integration' session adds no test proving the Celery task executes (all tests patch .delay and the task itself only prints), so end-to-end integration of the new dependency is unverified.

strengths: Solid trigger-coverage test suite: idempotency (no re-trigger on already-completed), correct-owner targeting, and no-notification on non-completing transitions are all tested.
Idempotency guard prevents duplicate notifications on repeated 'completed' updates.
get_user_by_id mirrors the existing get_user_by_username/get_db access pattern, showing partial pattern adherence in the core app.
Configuration is environment-variable driven with sane defaults, and Celery app/config are cleanly separated into their own modules.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-tested but architecturally over-built: a heavyweight Celery/Redis pipeline is bolted onto a simple synchronous app for a mocked email, and the 'completed' status alias introduces domain-state redundancy that worsens the codebase's overall fit.

problems.description: BaseRepository.update() and the table-name usage interpolate SQL identifiers via f-strings (`f"{col} = ?"`); safe only while column names are literal kwargs from internal callers, but fragile and a mild injection smell if ever wired to external input.
BaseRepository.update() performs three round trips per call (existence check, UPDATE, re-read), where the original update_task did one conditional UPDATE plus a read.

Repositories are module-level singletons constructed at import time in app.py; the get_db callable indirection keeps them safe against the test suite's runtime DATABASE swap, but it does create an import-time coupling between app and the repository layer.

The new repositories.py adds one measured convention violation ('Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE', likely the lowercase `table` class attributes); the remaining violations in app.py/celery_app.py/celery_config.py/conftest.py are pre-existing in files this commit does not touch.

strengths: Introduces a cohesive repository layer that removes duplicated SQL from app.py while preserving exact behavior (partial field updates, IntegrityError handling, None on missing record).
Injecting get_db as a callable rather than importing it preserves the runtime DATABASE swap the test suite relies on — an existing pattern respected, not broken.
Clean style per repo conventions: snake_case functions, PascalCase classes, type hints on public signatures, dataclass-like dict returns.
Measured net improvement: cognitive complexity -2 and duplication -0.6% with no new bugs or smells on the AST delta.
commit_reviews.summary: A behavior-preserving repository-layer refactor that meaningfully reduces duplication and respects the existing get_db test seam, with only minor new smells (dynamic SQL f-strings, 3-round-trip update) — the 0.70 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files, which is the discrepancy to note against the measurement.

problems.description: find_page_by_owner() runs a COUNT(*) over all of the owner's tasks on every page request to return `total` — an O(n) scan that adds cost even when the client never reads the total. Acceptable for this app's size, but unbounded as the table grows.

rate_limit_key() re-decodes and re-verifies the JWT that require_auth has already validated on the same request — duplicated crypto work per request; could derive the key from g.user_id set by the auth decorator.

The Limiter hardcodes redis://localhost:6379/0 as the fallback storage URI. If Redis is unavailable the app's routes fail outright (no in-memory fallback), coupling every endpoint to a running Redis instance beyond the sqlite dependency already present.

Mechanical convention score is 0.70 with 16 violations, but most are in pre-existing files outside this commit (celery_app.py, celery_config.py); the new code here is consistently snake_case functions and UPPER_CASE constants. Discrepancy with the score noted.

strengths: Correct keyset pagination: the limit+1 probe makes next_cursor None exactly when the page is last, and ordering by id DESC avoids the off-by-one/missed-row pitfalls of naive OFFSET pagination.
Clean layering — pagination lives in the repository (find_page_by_owner), response shaping in the route handler, rate limiting at the app boundary.
Redis key_prefix namespacing plus application_limits with a global scope shows real understanding of shared-storage collision risk and per-endpoint bucket semantics.
The conftest fixture that resets limiter counters per test isolates tests from shared Redis state — pragmatic and correct.
Updated existing tests to the new envelope response shape and added a JSON 429 handler, keeping the API surface consistent.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects the existing repository/route patterns and ships with tests, with only minor performance and dependency concerns.

compounding_issues: Session 2 committed __pycache__/*.pyc build artifacts into git; they persisted and produced noisy diffs in every later commit (sessions 3-5 all touch changing .pyc files).

Session 3 introduced a third status 'completed' as an alias to 'done' to trigger email notifications without altering existing behavior — but the notification fires only on transition to 'completed', so a user marking a task 'done' (the natural completion state) silently gets no email, leaving the semantics ambiguous.
Rate-limiter storage is hardcoded to localhost:6379 and SECRET_KEY defaults to a hardcoded dev key; acceptable in the story sandbox but both would need env-guards before any real deployment.
key_decisions: Repository pattern with connection-factory injection (session 4): all SQLite access extracted into repositories.py, routes never touch the DB directly, and get_db is passed at call time so tests can still swap DATABASE after import.
JWT auth with werkzeug password hashing (session 2) became the backbone of the system — session 5's rate limiter keys per-user off the JWT user_id, and the owner_id migration ties ownership to auth.
Celery-based async email notification triggered on transition to a new 'completed' alias status (session 3), deliberately not touching the pre-existing 'pending'/'done' behavior.
Forward-compatible schema migration (_migrate_add_owner_id) for databases created before auth existed (session 2-3 boundary).
Flask-Limiter with per-app key prefixing plus an autouse conftest fixture that resets limiter counters before every test — shared-Redis test isolation handled at the outset of session 5.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and meaningfully across all five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean single-file CRUD baseline with a real test suite; session 2 layered on secure JWT auth with proper password hashing, growing tests from 14 to 33; session 3 added async Celery notifications with a dedicated test module; session 4 was a behavior-preserving refactor to the Repository pattern that shrank app.py by ~74 lines while the existing 42 tests passed unchanged (the low point, since no new tests were added and confidence dipped to 0.73); session 5 was the strongest, adding rate limiting and pagination with two new 150-200-line test modules plus an autouse rate-limiter reset fixture, recovering confidence and ending at 65 passing tests across 495 code lines. Test discipline stayed high throughout (test/code ratio ~1.3 at the end), and all 65 tests pass at the final commit.
story_review.summary: A textbook multi-session progression — build, secure, integrate, refactor, harden — executed coherently with strong test discipline and a final fully-green suite, marred only by minor hygiene (tracked .pyc files) and one semantically ambiguous completion-status alias.
